lessons.title: The Haber process and NPK fertilisers
lessons.summary: Learn how ammonia is manufactured from nitrogen and hydrogen, why the conditions chosen are a compromise between yield, rate and cost, and how ammonia is turned into the fertilisers that feed the world.
objectives: I can describe the raw materials, conditions and equation for the Haber process.
I can explain why 450 °C, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst are used as a compromise (Higher).
I can interpret graphs of yield against temperature and pressure (Higher).
I can explain what NPK fertilisers are and why plants need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
I can describe how ammonium salts, phosphate rock products and potassium salts are obtained for fertilisers.

activities.title: Making ammonia
activities.content:
## Nitrogen from the air, hydrogen from gas

**Ammonia, NH₃**, is one of the most important chemicals made in the world, mainly because it is the starting point for **nitrogen fertilisers**. It is made by the **Haber process**.

### Raw materials

- **Nitrogen** is obtained from the **air** (which is 78% nitrogen), usually by fractional distillation of liquid air or by removing the oxygen.
- **Hydrogen** is obtained from **natural gas (methane)** by reacting it with steam.

### The reaction

The purified gases are mixed in a 1 : 3 ratio and passed over a catalyst:

**N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)**

The ⇌ symbol tells you the reaction is **reversible**: as ammonia forms, some of it breaks back down into nitrogen and hydrogen. The forward reaction is **exothermic**.

### Conditions

| Condition | Value |
|---|---|
| temperature | about **450 °C** |
| pressure | about **200 atmospheres** |
| catalyst | **iron** |

### Collecting the product

The mixture leaving the reactor is **cooled**. Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than nitrogen or hydrogen, so it **liquefies** and is drained off. The **unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen** are **recycled** back into the reactor, so nothing is wasted. Only about 15% of the gases react on each pass, but with recycling the overall conversion is high.

question.text: Complete the sentences about the Haber process.

activities.title: Choosing the conditions (Higher)
activities.content:
## A compromise between yield, rate and cost

Because the reaction is reversible, it reaches an **equilibrium**. Le Chatelier's principle says the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose any change made to it.

### Temperature

The forward reaction is **exothermic**. A **low temperature** would push the equilibrium **towards ammonia**, giving a **higher yield**. But at low temperature the **rate** is far too slow: it would take days to reach equilibrium.

A **high temperature** gives a fast rate but a **low yield**, because the equilibrium shifts towards the reactants.

**450 °C is a compromise**: a reasonable yield produced at an acceptable rate.

### Pressure

There are **4 molecules of gas on the left** (1 N₂ + 3 H₂) and only **2 on the right** (2 NH₃). Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **fewer molecules**, so **high pressure increases the yield** of ammonia. High pressure also increases the rate.

So why not use 1000 atmospheres? Very high pressures need **thick-walled, expensive pipes and reactors**, use a lot of **energy** to compress the gases, and are a **safety** risk.

**200 atmospheres is a compromise** between a good yield and the cost and danger of the equipment.

### Catalyst

The **iron catalyst** speeds up both the forward and backward reactions equally. It does **not change the yield**; it just makes equilibrium arrive faster, which means a lower temperature can be used than would otherwise be needed.

### The recurring exam phrase

"The conditions are a **compromise** between **yield**, **rate** and **cost**."

activities.title: Worked example: reading a yield graph (Higher)
activities.content:
**The table gives the percentage yield of ammonia at equilibrium under different conditions.**

| Pressure (atm) | 350 °C | 450 °C | 550 °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 38% | 17% | 8% |
| 200 | 52% | 28% | 13% |
| 400 | 66% | 40% | 21% |

**Question 1: What happens to the yield as temperature rises at a fixed pressure?**

Reading along any row, the yield **falls** as temperature increases (at 200 atm: 52% → 28% → 13%). This is because the forward reaction is **exothermic**, so higher temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the reactants.

**Question 2: What happens as pressure rises at a fixed temperature?**

Reading down any column, the yield **rises** (at 450 °C: 17% → 28% → 40%). Higher pressure favours the side with **fewer gas molecules**, which is the ammonia side.

**Question 3: The highest yield in the table is 66%. Why is this not the condition used?**

350 °C would make the **rate too slow**, and 400 atm would need very **expensive, strong equipment** and more energy for compression. The industrial choice of 450 °C and 200 atm gives 28% per pass, which with **recycling** is perfectly economic.

**Skill:** always describe the trend, then explain it using equilibrium, then link to the compromise.

question.text: Higher tier. Why is a temperature of 450 °C used in the Haber process rather than a lower temperature that would give a higher yield?
question.hint: What happens to the rate at a low temperature?
question.explanation: A lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield because the forward reaction is exothermic, but the rate would be far too slow. 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate.

options.text: At lower temperatures the rate of reaction would be too slow.
At lower temperatures the yield would be lower.
options.feedback: The yield would actually be higher; the problem is the rate.

options.text: The iron catalyst only works above 450 °C.
Ammonia decomposes below 450 °C.

question.text: Higher tier. Which statements about the effect of pressure in the Haber process are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Count the gas molecules on each side, and think about equipment.
question.explanation: Higher pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia because there are fewer gas molecules on the right, so the yield rises. Very high pressures are avoided because the equipment is expensive and there are safety risks.

options.text: Increasing the pressure increases the yield of ammonia.
Very high pressures are not used because the equipment would be expensive and less safe.
Pressure has no effect because the reaction is reversible.
options.feedback: Pressure affects any gas equilibrium with unequal numbers of molecules on each side.

options.text: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the reactants.
options.feedback: It shifts towards the side with fewer gas molecules, which is the ammonia side.

activities.title: NPK fertilisers
activities.content:
## Feeding plants

Plants need three elements in large amounts to grow well:

| Element | Symbol | Needed for |
|---|---|---|
| **nitrogen** | N | making proteins and chlorophyll, leafy growth |
| **phosphorus** | P | root growth, DNA, energy transfer |
| **potassium** | K | flowering, fruit, disease resistance |

Crops take these elements out of the soil, and harvesting removes them from the field. **Fertilisers** put them back so that farmers can grow more food on the same land.

### NPK fertilisers

An **NPK fertiliser** is a **formulation** of compounds containing all three elements in **soluble** forms, so that plants can absorb them through their roots. The numbers on the bag (for example 20-10-10) give the percentages of N, P and K.

The compounds used are:

- **Nitrogen**: ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate, ammonium phosphate, and sometimes urea.
- **Phosphorus**: compounds made from phosphate rock.
- **Potassium**: potassium chloride and potassium sulfate, which are **mined** directly.

### Natural versus manufactured

Manure and compost provide the same elements but slowly and in variable amounts. Manufactured fertilisers are **concentrated** and their composition is **known exactly**, so the farmer can match the fertiliser to the crop. The trade-off is the energy and raw materials used to make them, and the risk of soluble nitrates washing into rivers.

activities.title: Worked example: making ammonium nitrate
activities.content:
**Describe how ammonia is turned into ammonium nitrate fertiliser.**

**Step 1: make nitric acid.**

Some of the ammonia is **oxidised** (reacted with oxygen over a catalyst) and dissolved in water to make **nitric acid, HNO₃**.

**Step 2: neutralise.**

Ammonia is an **alkali** and nitric acid is an acid, so mixing them is a **neutralisation** reaction:

NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃

ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate

**Step 3: obtain the solid.**

In the laboratory you could crystallise the salt by evaporating the water. In industry, the reaction is done with concentrated reagents and the heat released **evaporates the water**, so the salt forms directly and is made into pellets.

**Why is ammonium nitrate a good fertiliser?**

Both the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, and the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, contain nitrogen, so the compound is rich in nitrogen (35% by mass), and it is very **soluble**, so plants absorb it quickly.

**The same pattern** with sulfuric acid gives ammonium sulfate, and with phosphoric acid gives ammonium phosphate, which supplies both N and P.

question.text: Match each acid to the ammonium salt formed when it is neutralised by ammonia.
question.hint: The salt takes its name from the acid.
question.explanation: Nitric acid gives ammonium nitrate, sulfuric acid gives ammonium sulfate, phosphoric acid gives ammonium phosphate.

activities.title: Phosphate rock and potassium
activities.content:
## The P and the K

### Phosphorus from phosphate rock

**Phosphate rock** is mined, but it cannot be used directly as a fertiliser because it is **insoluble**: plants cannot absorb it. It must be reacted with an acid to make **soluble** phosphate salts.

| Acid used | Products | Name |
|---|---|---|
| nitric acid | phosphoric acid + calcium nitrate | (the phosphoric acid is then neutralised with ammonia to give ammonium phosphate) |
| sulfuric acid | calcium sulfate + calcium phosphate | **single superphosphate** |
| phosphoric acid | calcium phosphate only | **triple superphosphate** |

You do not need to memorise every equation, but you should be able to say that phosphate rock is treated with an acid to make soluble phosphates, and name the acids.

### Potassium from mines

**Potassium chloride** and **potassium sulfate** occur naturally as **soluble** minerals, left behind when ancient seas evaporated. They are simply **mined** and used directly, with no chemical processing beyond crushing and purifying.

### Putting it together

An NPK fertiliser factory therefore has three inputs: ammonium salts from the **Haber process** plus acids, phosphates from **phosphate rock plus acid**, and **mined potassium salts**. They are blended into granules in the right proportions for a given crop.

question.text: Put the steps in order to show how nitrogen from the air ends up in ammonium nitrate fertiliser.
question.hint: Ammonia must be made before it can be used to make either the acid or the salt.
question.explanation: Nitrogen is separated from air, reacted with hydrogen in the Haber process to give ammonia, some ammonia is oxidised to nitric acid, and the acid is neutralised with more ammonia to give ammonium nitrate.

question.text:
Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). The forward reaction is exothermic.

(a) State the source of each raw material.

(b) State the temperature, pressure and catalyst used.

(c) **Higher tier:** Explain why a high pressure is used, and why the pressure is not made even higher.

(d) **Higher tier:** Explain why the temperature used is described as a compromise.

(e) Describe what happens to the gases leaving the reactor.
question.hint: Air and methane. 450 °C, 200 atm, iron. Fewer molecules on the right. Yield versus rate. Cooling and recycling.
question.explanation: (a) Nitrogen from the air; hydrogen from natural gas (methane). (b) About 450 °C, about 200 atmospheres, iron catalyst. (c) There are fewer gas molecules on the right, so high pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia and increases the yield (and rate); higher pressures would need very expensive, strong equipment and be less safe. (d) A lower temperature would give a higher yield because the reaction is exothermic, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C balances yield against rate. (e) The gases are cooled so the ammonia liquefies and is removed; unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.

markScheme.criterion: Nitrogen from the air; hydrogen from natural gas / methane
High pressure increases yield because there are fewer molecules of gas on the product side (equilibrium shifts right)
Even higher pressure would need expensive equipment / be unsafe / cost too much energy
Lower temperature gives higher yield (exothermic) but rate too slow; compromise between yield and rate
Gases cooled so ammonia liquefies and is removed; unreacted gases recycled

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Haber process**: N₂ (from air) + 3H₂ (from natural gas) ⇌ 2NH₃, at about **450 °C**, **200 atm**, **iron catalyst**. Ammonia is cooled and liquefied; unreacted gases are **recycled**.
- Higher: the reaction is reversible and exothermic. **Low temperature** raises yield but slows the rate; **high pressure** raises yield (fewer gas molecules on the right) but costs money and safety. The conditions are a **compromise between yield, rate and cost**. The catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield.
- **NPK fertilisers** are formulations supplying soluble **nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium** for plant growth.
- **Nitrogen**: ammonia neutralises nitric, sulfuric or phosphoric acid to give **ammonium nitrate, sulfate or phosphate**.
- **Phosphorus**: insoluble **phosphate rock** is treated with nitric, sulfuric or phosphoric acid to make soluble phosphates (superphosphates).
- **Potassium**: potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are **mined** and used directly.

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier. The iron catalyst in the Haber process does not increase the yield of ammonia. Explain why it is still used.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does a catalyst do to the rate, and what does that allow the operators to do with the temperature?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield. However, it allows equilibrium to be reached much faster, and it means a lower temperature can be used than would otherwise be needed, which gives a better yield and saves energy.

markScheme.criterion: Catalyst speeds up both forward and backward reactions equally so does not change the equilibrium position
It increases the rate so ammonia is produced faster / equilibrium reached sooner
Allows a lower temperature to be used, which gives a higher yield / saves energy

practiceQuestions.text:
A student makes ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by adding ammonia solution to dilute sulfuric acid.

(a) Write the word equation for the reaction, and name the type of reaction.

(b) Describe how the student could obtain dry crystals of ammonium sulfate from the solution.

(c) Explain one difference between how the salt is made in the laboratory and how it is made on an industrial scale.
practiceQuestions.hint: Alkali plus acid. Evaporate and crystallise. Industry uses concentrated reagents in a continuous process.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) ammonia + sulfuric acid → ammonium sulfate; neutralisation. (b) Heat the solution gently to evaporate some of the water, then leave it to cool so crystals form; filter and dry them. (c) In industry the reaction is carried out continuously with concentrated reagents and the heat of reaction evaporates the water directly, whereas in the laboratory dilute solutions are used in small batches and the product is crystallised separately.

markScheme.criterion: Evaporate some water then allow to cool and crystallise (and dry)
Industry uses continuous process / concentrated reagents / heat of reaction evaporates the water / much larger scale
